questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Define what it means for a narrator to be reliable
questions.stem: In the memo on the old tram sheds the planner argues from a novel she is reading; what does it mean to call the voice in that novel reliable?

options.text: The narrator's account can be trusted to report events as they actually happened
The narrator is free from prejudice, so nothing in the account distorts the events
options.misconception: treats reliability as moral blamelessness only

options.text: The narrator tells the reader everything, so no information is withheld from us
options.misconception: equates reliability with total disclosure

options.text: The narrator's judgement is correct, so the reader should accept the narrator's opinions
options.misconception: confuses reliability with the narrator being right

questions.explanation: Reliability concerns whether a narrator's account can be trusted to represent events as they happened. It is not the same as moral innocence, total disclosure or being right about everything.
questions.hint: Ask what the account claims to report.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify textual evidence that a narrator is unreliable

stimulus.body: In a note on the market square traffic scheme, the planner cites a memoir chapter in which the writer insists that the market was always empty by four o'clock, while the market traders' own records show busy stalls until six.

questions.stem: In the market square memo the planner weighs the memoir against the traders' records; which detail best shows the narrator as unreliable?

options.text: The writer uses the first person throughout the chapter, so the account is biased
options.misconception: assumes first person narration makes a text unreliable

options.text: The writer's claim about closing time conflicts with the traders' records for the same year
The chapter recalls the market in detail, which shows the writer was inventing detail
options.misconception: treats vivid detail as evidence of invention

options.text: The chapter is written in the past tense, which shows the writer was not there at all
options.misconception: infers absence from the grammatical tense

questions.explanation: Unreliability is shown by the gap between what a narrator asserts and what other evidence supports. Tense, person and vividness of detail are not themselves signs of unreliability.
questions.hint: Look for a clash with outside evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how free indirect discourse blends two voices
questions.stem: At the council office the planner explains to a colleague how a novelist can put a character's thoughts into a narrator's own voice.

answer.exemplar: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's voice with a character's thoughts, dropping quotation marks and tags so that the sentences read as narration while carrying the character's judgement and vocabulary. The reader hears the character's mind without the page announcing it, which puts the two voices briefly in the same breath.

questions.explanation: Free indirect discourse mixes the narrator's voice with a character's thought without quotation marks or tags. The effect is intimacy: the reader hears the character's judgement inside the narration.
questions.hint: Look for a character's phrasing inside narration.

questions.stem: In the memo on the grain exchange conversion the planner quotes a line and asks which reading shows free indirect discourse at work.

options.text: The passage is written in the third person, so no character's thought is present at all
options.misconception: assumes third person rules out free indirect discourse

options.text: The sentence ends with a full stop, so the narration is clearly not interrupted
options.misconception: reads punctuation marks as proof of mode

options.text: The passage contains a direct question, so the character's voice is quoted rather than blended
options.misconception: treats any question mark as evidence of quoting

options.text: The sentence carries the character's impatient phrasing inside the narrator's grammatical third person

questions.explanation: Free indirect discourse shows itself when a character's distinctive phrasing appears inside the narrator's grammar without quotation or tags. Tense, punctuation and the mere presence of speech do not settle it.
questions.hint: Listen for whose phrasing sits inside the narration.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what focalisation limits a reader can perceive
questions.stem: During the river walk resurfacing meeting the planner reads a paragraph and asks what the paragraph actually lets the reader see.

options.text: It shows the world only as the character perceives it, so what lies outside that view stays hidden
It shows the world in full detail, so the reader knows more than the character does
options.misconception: confuses focalisation with narratorial omniscience

options.text: It shows nothing of the character's mind, so the scene is presented as bare record
options.misconception: reads focalisation as absence of viewpoint

options.text: It shows what other characters privately think, so the reader gathers several minds at once
options.misconception: treats focalisation as access to all minds

questions.explanation: Focalisation is the limit of what the narration lets us perceive, usually one character's view. It is not the same as omniscience, bare record or access to several minds at once.
questions.hint: Ask whose eyes the passage uses.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Define a focalisation shift within a narration
questions.stem: In the memo on the library opening hours the planner describes a change in the novel's point of view partway through a chapter.

options.text: The narration begins with one character and later carries a different character's viewpoint
options.misconception: treats a shift as a change of character entirely

options.text: The narration moves from one character's viewpoint to another's within the same scene
The narration begins outside the story and later enters a character's thoughts
options.misconception: describes a shift from outside to inside, not between people

options.text: The narration stops describing places and begins describing events in more detail
options.misconception: confuses a focalisation shift with a change of subject

questions.explanation: A focalisation shift is a change in whose viewpoint governs the narration. It may move between characters, and it is distinct from moving from outside to inside or from place to event.
questions.hint: Ask whose view we are seeing it through.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a setting can carry emotional weight

stimulus.body: In a note on the civic hall roof repair, the planner argues that the novel's description of the hall's leaking skylight is more than local colour, since it appears every time the protagonist is about to confess something.

questions.stem: In the civic hall memo the planner argues about the skylight; which claim about the setting carries the weight best?

options.text: The skylight shows the author took care with the building's real architectural history
options.misconception: reads the setting as background realism only

options.text: The skylight is a symbol of civic corruption, so the building stands for the council
options.misconception: insists the setting carries one fixed symbolic meaning

options.text: The leaking skylight recurs at the moments of pressure, so the place registers the emotion
The skylight is used twice in the novel, which proves the author planned the whole plot
options.misconception: treats repetition count as proof of planning

questions.explanation: A setting carries emotional weight through its recurrence at significant moments, so the place registers what the character cannot state. Symbolism, realism and repetition counts are secondary observations.
questions.hint: Ask when the detail returns in the story.

questions.learningObjective: State how a text signals a reliable narrator
questions.stem: In the bus depot relocation study the planner writes about a witness giving evidence in the novel's opening chapter.

options.misconception: defines reliability as emotional absence

options.misconception: defines reliability by grammatical person

options.misconception: requires other characters to confirm the narrator

options.text: A reliable narrator is one whose account of events the text gives no reason to doubt

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Describe the evidence needed to argue unreliability
questions.stem: At the neighbourhood archive digitisation meeting the planner explains how she would show a committee that a witness is unreliable.

answer.exemplar: She would point to a gap between what the witness asserts and what the rest of the text supports, such as a contradicted time, a missing motive or a detail that other characters contradict, and she would set those moments side by side. That kind of internal evidence, rather than a general impression of the writer's tone, is what establishes unreliability.

questions.explanation: An unreliable narrator is established by evidence within the text: contradictions, gaps and clashes with what other characters say. A vague sense of tone or bias is not proof.
questions.hint: Set the claims against the rest of the text.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what blending the voices achieves for a reader
questions.stem: In the high street tree planting note the planner explains why a novelist would blur the voices of narrator and character.

options.text: To make the novel's facts harder to check, since blurred voices leave nothing certain

options.text: To let a character's thinking press close to the reader without a formal announcement of it

options.text: To give the novel two speakers who can contradict each other on the same page
options.misconception: treats blending as a device for contradiction

questions.explanation: Blurring the voices lets a character's thinking press close to the reader without being announced as speech or thought. It is not about obscuring facts, avoiding description or staging contradiction.
questions.hint: Think about closeness, not confusion.

options.misconception: claims narrators never use the present tense

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a focalisation that rests on selection alone

stimulus.body: In a memo on the towpath resurfacing, the planner quotes a scene in which a council porter narrates the state of the path in plain terms, without any comment on what he thinks of the residents who use it.

questions.stem: In a second towpath memo the planner asks how the porter's narration is focalised; which reading is best?

options.text: The scene is not focalised, because the porter never reveals what he is thinking
options.misconception: requires interior access before a view can count

options.text: The scene is focalised on the residents, since the path matters most to them
options.misconception: focalises on the affected rather than the perceiver

options.text: The scene is focalised on the council, since the porter works for the council
options.misconception: assumes employment determines the focaliser

options.text: The scene is focalised on the porter, whose priorities select what the reader notices

questions.explanation: A viewpoint can be established by selection alone, so the porter's attention and priorities filter what we see. Interior access, the affected parties and the speaker's employer do not decide it.
questions.hint: Ask whose attention shapes the detail.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to demonstrate a shift of viewpoint
questions.stem: In the footbridge study the planner explains to a committee how she would show that a viewpoint changes inside a single chapter.

answer.exemplar: She would point to the change in what is noticed, because a shift of focalisation is marked by one observer's priorities giving way to another's within the same scene, often signalled by a fresh attention to an object already in view. Describing the place differently, or simply telling the committee the viewpoint has moved, would not be evidence enough to show it.

questions.explanation: A focalisation shift is demonstrated by a change in what the narration notices. New wording, an announced change of viewpoint or a shift of subject are weaker or misleading proofs.
questions.hint: Show the change in what is noticed.

questions.learningObjective: Assess the rhetorical effect of a trustworthy sounding voice
questions.stem: During the depot consultation the planner considers what a narrator gains by sounding entirely trustworthy.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a credible voice leaves the reader no room to judge the story
options.misconception: believes credibility removes the reader's judgement

questions.learningObjective: Identify free indirect discourse in a quoted sentence

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early passages often reveal less of a setting
questions.stem: During the promenade study the planner explains why a novel's opening pages often tell us less about a place than its later pages do.

answer.exemplar: Because the opening pages are usually filtered through a first observer's limited purposes, so only what concerns that person is registered, and later the narration widens or changes hands to show the same district from other needs and other interests. The difference in what is described is a difference in who is describing and what they are there to find.

questions.explanation: Early passages are filtered through one observer's purposes, so they record less of the place. The change comes from who is observing and what they want, not from the setting itself.
questions.hint: Think about who is looking in each passage.

options.misconception: explains the change as a shift of place

options.text: The change is a focalisation shift, since each observer selects a different set of details

questions.explanation: A focalisation shift shows in the selection of detail, so the same foyer yields different accounts. Word choice, period and place are changes of a different order.
questions.hint: Ask which details each observer picks out.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Set out an argument that a witness is unreliable
questions.stem: At the conservation panel the planner explains how she argued that a witness in a local history was unreliable.

answer.exemplar: She set the witness's account against three things the text itself supplies: the year he gives, which the title page contradicts, a route he says he walked, which the geography will not allow, and a claim that another character repeats back to him in different words. Each discrepancy narrows the area in which his version can be trusted, which is how unreliability is argued rather than asserted.

questions.explanation: Unreliability is argued by accumulating specific discrepancies between the account and the text's own evidence. Asserting that a witness seems biased proves nothing.
questions.hint: Gather the specific discrepancies.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a writer's tone does not settle a narrator's credibility
questions.stem: In the harbour wall note the planner explains why a narrator's credibility cannot be settled by the writer's own tone.

answer.exemplar: Because the writer's tone belongs to the writer and not to the voice the reader is judging, a smooth or anxious narration tells us nothing reliable about how far to trust that narrator's account. The test has to be made inside the text, by setting the account against what the text itself establishes, so that any partiality shows in what is claimed and what is passed over.

questions.explanation: A writer's tone is not evidence about a narrator's trustworthiness, since it belongs to the writer. The test must be made inside the text, against what the text establishes.
questions.hint: Judge the voice, not the writer's manner.

questions.explanation: A careful account that is silent where it matters most is best described as reliable within its limits and silent elsewhere. Extending one omission, assuming general soundness and judging tone are not warranted.
questions.hint: Ask where the account is silent, and when.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Propose a way to test a vivid witness account
questions.stem: In the aqueduct memo the planner asks how a committee can test a witness whose account sounds vivid.

options.text: Ask how many times the witness has told the story before, since repetition causes distortion
options.misconception: blames the number of retellings for distortion

options.text: Compare the specific details against records that can be checked independently
Ask whether the witness seems pleased with the account, since pleasure suggests invention
options.misconception: reads the witness's manner as a sign

options.text: Ask how long the interview lasted, since longer interviews lose more detail
options.misconception: links interview length to accuracy

questions.explanation: A vivid account is best tested against independently checkable records. Repetition, the witness's manner and the length of an interview are not evidence about accuracy.
questions.hint: Check the specifics against a record.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare a quoted voice with a blended one
questions.stem: During the bus interchange consultation the planner compares a novel that quotes its characters with one that blends their voices.

options.text: The blended novel is more realistic, since real speech is never neatly punctuated in fiction
options.misconception: claims realism depends on punctuation habits

options.text: The quoted novel is more revealing, since a quoted line shows the exact words used
options.misconception: assumes quoted speech is always more revealing

options.text: The blended novel draws the reader nearer, since the character's thinking is felt rather than reported
The two novels are indistinguishable, since readers always reconstruct the same meaning
options.misconception: claims readers always derive identical meanings

questions.explanation: Blending lets the reader feel the character's thinking inside the narration, which draws them nearer. Realism, the superiority of quoted lines and identical reading are not the differences.
questions.hint: Think about feeling rather than reporting.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Free indirect discourse identified in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Weigh competing readings of a single blended sentence
questions.stem: Under the lamp outside the town hall the planner weighs two claims about a single blended sentence in a novel.

options.text: The sentence is a quotation, since the words keep the rhythm of spoken delivery
options.misconception: treats rhythm as proof of quotation

options.text: The sentence is objective, since no speaker is named as the source of the judgement
options.misconception: treats an unnamed judgement as objectivity

options.text: The sentence proves the narrator has no opinion, since the tone is so evenly balanced
options.misconception: infers narrator neutrality from balanced tone

options.text: The sentence may be read either way, so the pattern across the passage must decide it

questions.explanation: A single sentence can be read as narration or as a blend, so the pattern across the passage is what settles the question. Rhythm, objective tone and narrator neutrality do not.
questions.hint: One sentence is not enough to decide.
